lesson.text: Quick memory: what does a router do? (It joins devices and sends messages the right way.) Today: finding things on the web with a search engine.
A search engine doesn't read the whole web when you ask. Its programs visit pages all the time and build an index: a giant list of which words are on which pages. Your search looks in that index.
Choose keywords: the few words that matter most. Instead of Please tell me how tall a giraffe can grow, search giraffe height. Leave out little words like the, a and please.
Be exact: bat could be an animal or a cricket bat. Search fruit bat or bat animal to find what you mean. Put words in quotation marks, like “blue whale”, to find them together, in that order.
Results are ranked: the pages the search engine guesses are most useful come first. It looks at how well your words match, and at how many other pages link to each page.
The first result is not always the best or the truest. Some results at the top are adverts, marked Ad or Sponsored. Read a few results before you choose.
Search safely: a grown-up can set up a search made for children. If something upsetting appears, close it and tell a grown-up you trust.
Try it in the world: think of a question about our world, like how volcanoes form. Write three different searches for it and choose the best keywords. Next: checking whether what you find is true.

exercises.prompt: Which are the best keywords to find out how fast a cheetah runs?
exercises.hint: Which words matter most for your question?
exercises.explain: cheetah speed: the two words that matter, and nothing extra.

exercises.prompt: The first search result is always the truest.
exercises.hint: How does the search engine order its results?
exercises.explain: False: results are ranked by guesses, and some at the top are adverts. Read a few.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a keyword, or a little word you can leave out?
exercises.hint: Does the word tell the search engine what you are looking for?
exercises.explain: giraffe, height and volcano matter. the, please and a don't.

exercises.prompt: What does a search engine look in when you search?
choices: its index of the pages it has visited
exercises.explain: It looks in its index: a list of which words are on which pages.

exercises.prompt: You search bat and get cricket bats. What should you search instead?
exercises.hint: Add a word that says which kind of bat you mean.
exercises.explain: bat animal tells the search engine which bat you mean.

exercises.prompt: What does Ad next to a search result mean?
exercises.hint: Why would a page be at the top without being the best?
choices: someone paid to put it there
exercises.explain: Ad (or Sponsored) means someone paid for it to be shown there. It may not be the best answer.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of a good search in order.
exercises.hint: Start with your question and end by checking.
items: Think what you want to find
Check the facts on another good site
exercises.explain: Think, choose keywords, search, read a few results, then check the facts somewhere else.

exercises.prompt: Match each search to what it finds.
exercises.hint: Quotation marks keep words together; more keywords make it narrower.
exercises.explain: “blue whale” finds the words together, whale finds every whale, blue whale size finds how big they are.

exercises.prompt: Search engines rank results: the ones they guess are most useful come first.
exercises.hint: Why are some results at the top?
exercises.explain: True: they are ranked, most useful (by the search engine's guess) first.

exercises.prompt: Why might a page be near the top of the results?
exercises.hint: What does the search engine look at when it ranks pages?
choices: many other pages link to it
exercises.explain: Pages that many other pages link to are often ranked higher. That still doesn't make them true.

exercises.prompt: Juno searched “volcanoes in Italy” with quotation marks and found few pages. What could help?
exercises.hint: What do the quotation marks do?
exercises.explain: Quotation marks find only those exact words in that order. Without them, pages with the words anywhere count.

exercises.prompt: Sort these search habits: do they help or not?
items: clicking the first result without reading
exercises.hint: Which habits find good, true answers?
exercises.explain: Reading a few results, checking another site and exact keywords help. The others don't.

exercises.prompt: Changing your keywords can give you better results.
exercises.hint: What decides which pages you get?
exercises.explain: True: better keywords find better pages. Try again with other words if the first search doesn't work.

exercises.prompt: What is a search engine's index?
exercises.hint: Remember what the search engine's programs build as they visit pages.
choices: a giant list of which words are on which pages
exercises.explain: The index is a giant list of which words are on which pages. Your search looks in it.

exercises.prompt: Sort the searches: well chosen, or could be better?
items: please tell me about the giraffe
exercises.hint: Good searches use the few words that matter, and are exact.
exercises.explain: Well chosen: giraffe height, fruit bat and volcanoes Italy are short, exact keywords. Could be better: the polite question has little words, bat could mean a cricket bat, and 'the and of a' has no keywords at all.
